---
title: "Joins, binding, and set operations"
---

## Joins

The join functions take the right-hand table as their first argument. The input
table is the left-hand table `x`.

| Function | Rows kept |
| --- | --- |
| `inner_join($y)` | Rows of x with a match in y |
| `left_join($y)` | All rows of x |
| `right_join($y)` | All rows of y |
| `full_join($y)` | All rows of both |
| `semi_join($y)` | Rows of x with a match, x's columns only |
| `anti_join($y)` | Rows of x without a match |
| `cross_join($y)` | Every combination |

`by:` names the key columns. A string or list joins on columns with the same
name in both tables, and an associative array maps differing names:
`by: ['school' => 'school_id']`. The forms mix, as in
`['id', 'code' => 'country_code']`. Without `by:`, the tables join on every
column they share.

{{< include ../examples/_joins.md >}}

The options follow dplyr 1.1:

- `suffix:` renames clashing non-key columns, `['.x', '.y']` by default.
- `keep: true` keeps y's key columns.
- `na_matches: 'never'` stops NA keys from matching. By default NA matches NA.
- `multiple:` is `'all'`, `'any'`, `'first'`, or `'last'`.
- `unmatched: 'error'` throws when rows would be dropped.
- `relationship:` checks `'one-to-one'`, `'one-to-many'`, `'many-to-one'`, or
  `'many-to-many'`. An unexpected many-to-many join raises dplyr's warning.

{{< include ../examples/_join-options.md >}}

Joins keep x's grouping, except for a grouping column that the join renames.

## join_by()

`join_by()` builds dplyr's join specifications. A string is an equality on
the same column name, `['a' => 'b']` maps names, and a comparison of two
`col()` expressions compares x's column (left) with y's (right). Every
condition must hold.

```php
join_by('id', col('t')->ge(col('start')), col('t')->lt(col('end')))
join_by('id', between('t', 'start', 'end'))        // start and end are y's columns
join_by('id', closest(col('t')->ge(col('start'))))  // the latest start at or before t
join_by(within('lo', 'hi', 'start', 'end'))         // x's interval inside y's
join_by(overlaps('lo', 'hi', 'start', 'end'))
```

For inequality, rolling, and overlap joins, `keep` defaults to dplyr's
behavior: equality keys are merged and the columns in other conditions are
kept from both tables. `keep: false` is an error for these joins. Database tables
run them in SQL, except right and full rolling joins, which load the rows.

`nest_join()` keeps every row of x and adds a list-column (`name:`, default
`'data'`) holding each row's matching rows of y as a table.

## Binding

`bind_rows()` stacks tables under the input one, matching columns by name and
filling missing columns with NA. `_id:` adds a column with each row's source.
`bind_cols()` puts tables side by side and renames duplicate names as
`name...position`.

{{< include ../examples/_bind.md >}}

## Set operations and row updates

`union()`, `union_all()`, `intersect()`, `setdiff()`, and `symdiff()` compare
whole rows. `setequal()` returns true when both tables hold the same distinct
rows.

The `rows_*()` functions modify the input table using another table's rows,
matched on `by:` (y's first column by default):

- `rows_insert()` adds rows with new keys; `conflict: 'ignore'` skips existing
  keys.
- `rows_append()` adds all rows.
- `rows_update()` overwrites values for matching keys.
- `rows_patch()` fills only NA values for matching keys.
- `rows_upsert()` updates matching keys and inserts new ones.
- `rows_delete()` removes matching keys.

`unmatched: 'ignore'` allows y keys that x lacks.

{{< include ../examples/_set-rows.md >}}
